 Nagpur in Safe Seismic Zone; Only Quakes of Magnitude 6 or Above May Pose Danger, Says GSI Chief 
 Trending Punjab Murder Kolkata Techie Assault Bareilly Suicide Diwali AQI Pawan Kalyan Delhi Red Fort Blast Punjab Murder Kolkata Techie Assault Bareilly Suicide Diwali AQI Pawan Kalyan Delhi Red Fort Blast Punjab Murder Kolkata Techie Assault Bareilly Suicide Diwali AQI Pawan Kalyan Delhi Red Fort Blast Nagpur in Safe Seismic Zone; Only Quakes of Magnitude 6 or Above May Pose Danger, Says GSI Chief 
 Sarfaraz Ahmed / Nov 12, 2026, 01:02 IST Save Comments Share Aa + Text Size Small
 Medium
 Large
 Print Dinesh Ganvir Nagpur: Seeking to allay fears triggered by recent low-intensity earthquakes in the region, Geological Survey of India (GSI) director general Dinesh Ganvir on Wednesday asserted that Nagpur falls in a low-risk seismic zone and there is no immediate cause for concern. “Only a major quake measuring 6 or above on the Richter scale is likely to cause significant damage,” said Ganvir, a Nagpur University alumnus who recently assumed charge as GSI chief. His reassurance comes against the backdrop of three earthquakes recorded in Nagpur and Yavatmal districts on Sunday and Monday. A 2.6-magnitude earthquake was recorded near Paradgaon lake, close to Umred, at 2.17pm on Oct 8, at a depth of 5km. On Oct 9, a 3.0-magnitude earthquake struck near Kalamb in Yavatmal district around 3pm, followed by a 1.9-magnitude tremor near Soholi, close to Khaparkheda, at 3.28pm. The latter originated at a depth of around 4km. Earlier, a 3.0-magnitude earthquake was recorded near Haldgaon and Dawaha in Umred tehsil on Oct 27. Though Nagpur falls under Seismic Zone II, the country’s lowest-risk category, the cluster of tremors across multiple locations has brought renewed attention to the region’s geological activity and intensified calls for closer scientific monitoring. The region recorded two seismic events in 2023 and 11 in 2024, sparking concern over the region’s seismic stability. “The tremors stem from the ongoing collision between the Indian Plate and the Eurasian Plate along the Main Himalayan Thrust. As the Indian Plate pushes northward, immense tectonic pressure builds up across the landmass. While this friction drives earthquakes along the Himalayan boundary, the resulting stress also travels inward, periodically triggering minor to moderate seismic activity across fault lines in Central India,” he explained. Ganvir said GSI had conducted field investigations in the Umred region following tremors reported last year. The team spent nearly two months studying the geological conditions and submitted a report examining the possible causes of the seismic activity. Speaking to the media at the GSI office here, Ganvir said the agency’s observatory transmits earthquake data to its head office in Kolkata, where it is processed and forwarded to the govt. Meanwhile, a GSI team has been conducting a separate microzonation study for nearly a month with the assistance of the state govt. The exercise will help identify localised seismic vulnerabilities and provide scientific inputs for disaster preparedness and infrastructure planning. The study is expected to be completed by January. The agency is also undertaking detailed geological investigations in Trimbakeshwar and surrounding areas of Nashik district ahead of the forthcoming Kumbh Mela. Ganvir also highlighted GSI’s role in identifying critical and strategic mineral resources under the Centre’s revised mineral exploration framework. Following amendments to the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act in 2020, the govt has accelerated exploration and auction of blocks containing critical minerals. Of the 100 blocks launched under the initiative, 72 have reportedly been taken forward so far, he said.
